claims.text: The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid and compositionally homogeneous.
Size-dependent surface-energy effects govern the onset and progression of the phase transition.
Surface compositional heterogeneity governs the onset and progression of the phase transition.
Premelting begins locally at heterogeneous surface regions.
After surface premelting begins, the molten region propagates inward until melting is complete.
Localized elemental segregation creates preferential sites for premelting.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles lowers the local melting temperature at their surfaces.
Compositional inhomogeneity lowers the local surface melting temperature.
Smaller FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will exhibit premelting at a lower temperature than nominally homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles with more pronounced surface segregation will exhibit premelting at a lower temperature than nominally homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
The nanoparticles will show premelting below the bulk melting temperature.
Melting will initiate at the particle surface and progress toward the core.
Nanoparticles with minimal surface defects or heterogeneity will exhibit a sharper, higher-temperature, more bulk-like melting transition without clear premelting features.
An inert argon atmosphere will limit oxidation and other side reactions during heating.
Controlled heating rates will minimize induced thermal gradients.
The proposed mechanism applies while particle sizes remain in the nanoregime where surface effects are significant.
In-situ TEM can be used to distinguish surface-initiated melting from core or spatially uniform melting.
DSC can be used to compare melting-onset temperatures and heat-flow characteristics between the sample sets.
Similar melting-onset temperatures in both sets together with no surface-initiated premelting would falsify the proposed governing role of size and surface composition.
